A synapse is a tiny junction — a point of communication — between two nerve cells (called neurons), or between a neuron and another type of cell (like a muscle cell). It is the place where a signal from one cell is passed on to the next. The word is used as a countable noun: you can have a synapse, many synapses, this synapse.
Why synapses exist

Your nervous system is built from billions of neurons. These neurons form long chains and networks to carry information — from your eyes to your brain, from your brain to your muscles, and everywhere in between. But here's the key fact: neurons don't physically touch each other. There is always a tiny gap between them. That gap, along with the structures on either side of it, is the synapse. The synapse is nature's solution to the problem of passing a signal across that gap.
The structure of a synapse

A synapse has three parts:

  1. The presynaptic terminal — the "sending" end. This is the tip of the neuron that is sending the signal. It contains tiny sacs called vesicles, which are filled with chemical messengers.
  2. The synaptic cleft — the gap itself. It is unimaginably small, about 20–40 nanometres wide (a nanometre is one billionth of a metre). Yet this tiny gap is where the magic of communication happens.
  3. The postsynaptic membrane — the "receiving" end. This is the surface of the next neuron (or cell), and it is studded with receptors — special protein structures that are designed to detect and respond to the chemical messengers from the other side.
How a synapse works

Signals travel through a neuron as electrical impulses. When an electrical impulse reaches the presynaptic terminal, it triggers the vesicles there to release their chemical messengers into the synaptic cleft. These chemical messengers are called neurotransmitters.

The neurotransmitters float across the cleft and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane — like a key fitting into a lock. When a neurotransmitter binds to its receptor, it causes a reaction in the receiving cell. Depending on the type of neurotransmitter and receptor involved, this reaction either:

  • Excites the next neuron — meaning it encourages that neuron to fire its own electrical signal and pass the message along, or
  • Inhibits the next neuron — meaning it suppresses that neuron from firing, essentially putting a brake on the signal.

After the neurotransmitters do their job, they are either broken down by enzymes in the cleft, or they are taken back up into the presynaptic neuron to be reused. This cleanup process is called reuptake.
Types of synapses

There are two main types:

Chemical synapses are the most common type, and they work exactly as described above — using neurotransmitters to carry the signal across the gap. They are slightly slower (a tiny fraction of a millisecond delay) because the signal has to convert from electrical to chemical and back to electrical.

Electrical synapses are less common. Here, the two cells are connected through protein channels called gap junctions, and the electrical signal passes directly from one cell to the other with no chemical step. These are faster but allow less control over the signal.
Common neurotransmitters

Since neurotransmitters are central to how synapses work, it helps to know the major ones:

  • Glutamate — the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter; it promotes the firing of signals and is crucial for learning and memory.
  • GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) — the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter; it calms neural activity and prevents overstimulation.
  • Dopamine — involved in pleasure, reward, motivation, and movement.
  • Serotonin — regulates mood, sleep, appetite, and emotional balance.
  • Acetylcholine — vital for muscle movement and also important in memory and attention.
  • Norepinephrine — involved in alertness, the stress response, and the "fight or flight" reaction.
Synapses and learning: plasticity

One of the most remarkable things about synapses is that they are not fixed. They can grow stronger or weaker over time based on how often they are used. This ability is called synaptic plasticity, and it is the biological foundation of learning and memory.

When two neurons repeatedly fire together — when a synapse is used over and over — it becomes more efficient. The connection strengthens: the presynaptic terminal releases more neurotransmitter, and the postsynaptic membrane grows more receptors. This is often summarised as "neurons that fire together, wire together."

Conversely, synapses that are rarely or never used weaken and can eventually disappear — a process called synaptic pruning. This is not a failure; it is the brain being efficient, removing connections it no longer needs. A lot of pruning happens during childhood and adolescence as the brain refines itself.

The formation of a new memory, the learning of a new skill, or even a habit you develop — all of these are, at the physical level, changes in synaptic strength and structure.
How many synapses does a human brain have?

The human brain is estimated to contain roughly 100 trillion synapses. That is more than all the stars in the Milky Way galaxy. This staggering number gives you a sense of the complexity of the brain's communication network — and why the brain is capable of such remarkable things.
Synapses in health and disease

Because synapses are the communication points of the entire nervous system, disruptions at the synapse have profound consequences. Many neurological and psychiatric conditions are, at their core, problems with synaptic function:

  • Parkinson's disease involves the death of neurons that produce dopamine, leading to fewer dopamine synapses in brain regions that control movement.
  • Depression is linked in part to reduced signalling at serotonin and norepinephrine synapses.
  • Alzheimer's disease involves the destruction of synapses in brain regions responsible for memory, which is why memory loss is its hallmark symptom.
  • Epilepsy involves uncontrolled, excessive firing across synapses in the brain.
  • Myasthenia gravis is a condition where the immune system attacks acetylcholine receptors at the synapses between neurons and muscle cells, causing muscle weakness.

Many medications work directly at synapses. Antidepressants like SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) block the reuptake of serotonin, keeping it in the synaptic cleft longer so it can have a stronger effect. Drugs like caffeine, nicotine, opioids, and many anaesthetics also work by interfering with synaptic signalling in specific ways.
In a sentence

If you had to capture the essence of the word in one sentence: a synapse is the specialised junction between neurons where the nervous system's electrical signals are converted into chemical messages and passed from one cell to the next — and in doing so, it makes possible every thought you think, every movement you make, every memory you hold, and every emotion you feel.
